translations.text: "Gird up your loins like a man."
The Holy Spirit, the spirit that surpasses every spirit, the spirit that illumined the Church in both its parts with the grace of wisdom and prophecy,
it is that spirit which uttered these words, through the man of God's grace, through long-suffering Job, saying:
"Gird up your loins like a man"; that is, it was in praise of that saint that God said to the demon:
"Have you considered my servant Job, that there is none like him on earth, a simple and upright man, fearing God and turning away from evil, and still keeping his innocence?"
To him the Lord said: "Gird up your loins like a man."
Holy Scripture is accustomed to call 'men' those who indeed follow the ways of the Lord with strong steps that do not falter.
Hence it is said in the psalm: "Act manfully, and let your heart be strengthened."
Hence Wisdom said in Proverbs: "O men, to you I cry out," as if she were saying openly:
"I do not speak to women, because those whose minds are unstable can in no way grasp my words."
To gird the loins is to restrain lust, whether in deed or in thought.
For the pleasure of the flesh lies in the loins. Hence it is also said to the holy preachers:
"Let your loins be girded, and burning lamps in your hands"; for by the loins lust is signified, and by the lamps the brightness of good works.
"They are therefore commanded to gird their loins and to hold lamps. It is as if" (he said that) they should hear openly:
"First restrain lust in yourselves, and then show others examples of good works from yourselves."
Many, then, of the saints and righteous ones, both under the Old Law and the New Testament, have fulfilled this teaching; that is,
they strengthened and bound their flesh, and they displayed many examples of their good deeds to peoples and to churches,
as did the radiance, the flame, the precious stone and the shining lamp, whose feast and commemoration falls at this season and time,
THAT IS, SAINT ADOMNÁN, that is, the noble holy priest, Adomnán.
Here, then, is told of his conversation with the demon, and of the demon's coming to Adomnán in human form, because the men of Munster had compelled him by force to come to Adomnán.
And this is how he came: with many questions. One of the questions was:
"Was it in form or without form that the devil sinned, and was it through knowledge or through ignorance that Adam sinned?"
"That is bold," said Adomnán. "Do not marvel," said the young warrior,
"it is one who knows who is speaking to you, for I was present at the [?] (shaping? event?)."
Adomnán looked at him angrily, and at once made the sign of the cross in his face.
Then the wretched one went out of their sight and left his stench in the assembly;
and the whole host recognised that it was a demon in human form that had come to lead their host astray.
And the name of God was glorified through Adomnán's driving him out.
Another time Adomnán was at the royal assembly of Conall and Cairpre at Ess Ruaid (Assaroe), enacting his Law.
A royal heir of the sons of Ainmire, that is, Flannabra son of Cumascach, came
with a woman prisoner whom he held captive because she had killed a woman, before Adomnán, and said to the cleric:
'Give a true judgement on this woman for killing the other woman.' Adomnán spoke, and his anger [?] flared:
'What else do you think should be done but to put her to death?' 'Who will put her to death?' said the young warrior.
'Someone whom no mother bore,' said Adomnán. 'That is me,' said the young warrior,
'for I was never born at all; I was taken out through my mother's side after she died.'
'I did not know of that exception to the rule,' said Adomnán,
'but all the same, God has saved the woman, and you will not go unpunished, for you yourself will die very soon,
and you will never obtain the kingship, and until Doomsday no man of your kindred will have a war-band of more than five men.'
Adomnán also took the kingship from the descendants of Dúngal son of Eladach of Cenél Lóegairi and gave it to the son of Fergus son of Ailill,
king of Uí Echach, after they had sworn a joint oath under Adomnán's hand.
(4) Adomnán also took the kingship from Irgalach grandson of Conaing and his descendants, because Irgalach had killed Niall son of Cernach in violation of Adomnán's protection.
Fínnachta son of Dúnchad, king of Tara, decreed
that the land of Colum Cille should have only the same status of freedom as the land of Patrick, Finnian and Ciarán, that is, that it should be brought into unfree status.
Adomnán was told about this, and it was not right before God,
for the men of Ireland had granted his land its freedom to Colum Cille because his kindred was nobler than that of any other saint in Ireland.
Adomnán said: 'Short will be the life of the king who made this decree, and he will be killed by his own kin,
and no one of his kindred will ever be a ruler, and no one bearing his name will hold the kingship of Tara.'
And all of that came to pass just so.
(5) Conall Oircnech son of Congal, king of Cenél Maine, said that he would not accept the Law of Adomnán.
His brother Conla said: 'If I were king, I would accept the Law.'
Conall mocked this because his brother was of little account. Adamnán said:
'Conall's life will be short, a death by firewood will carry him off, and there will never be a ruler of Tethba descended from him;
and Connla son of Congal will be ruler, and the rulership will come from him, unless he opposes this successor of mine.'
And so it came to pass.
Adamnán also took the kingship away from Cathusach son of Eochu, king of Dál Riata, and from his descendants forever.
Adamnán also took the kingship over the Uí Fhidgente away from Flaithbe of Cenél Mac nErca and from his descendants forever,
and gave it to Cenél Laippe of the Uí Echach of Munster, because Flaithbe had killed Dúngal son of Fergus.
(6) Another time Adamnán went into the territory of Leinster to contest Laíges of Telach Bregmann [?] against the community of Glendalough.
Cellach son of Gerthide was king of the Leinstermen at that time.
Dub Guala was abbot of Glendalough. Adamnán went to meet them on the assembly hill.
None of them rose before him, because the superior said it was not proper for him to rise before Adamnán, since he himself was a bishop and Adamnán only a priest.
Murchad son of Bran rose before him. He was a young lord at that time. Adamnán said to them:
'You have not been humble toward me in failing to rise for me, and you will not escape without penalty.
First, the bishop, who did not rise out of humility, will rise to commit a hateful sin, and he will persist in that sin until the day of his death, and he will die between the two hands of a harlot,
neither outdoors nor indoors, and he will go to hell, and it will not be long until then.
The king, moreover, will be driven from his kingship by the man who rose before me, that is, Murchad son of Bran.'
And he told Murchad to leave with him, for he would be killed if he stayed on the hill.
The Leinstermen came to Murchad and made him king, and Cellach went into exile to Congal son of Fergus, king of Tara.
Congal went with Cellach against the Leinstermen with the hosts of the Uí Néill, and they reached Fornocht.
Adamnán came from the territory of Connacht and joined them on that hill.
Adamnán told Congal not to make Cellach king against God's prohibition and against his own prohibition.
Congal said that they would settle the affairs of the churches as Adamnán wished, but that installing the king and ordering the people was his own business.
Adamnán said: 'In spite of that, Cellach will not be king, and there will never be a ruler of his kindred over the Leinstermen,
and each man of his descendants will be worse than the one before him.' He also said to Congal son of Fergus:
'You will not be king from today on, you will not reach your own land alive, a sudden death will carry you off, and there will never be a ruler descended from you.'
And everything came to pass as Adomnán had said.
(7) Once Adomnán was walking around the cemetery on Tory. The saint looked, blessed the cemetery and said:
'The body of a pregnant woman is in the cemetery, and her being in it is harmful to the saints. This here is her grave;
dig her up and take her with you to the seashore.' 'There are also,' said Adomnán,
'four people in the cemetery who, if they asked God for land in place of the sea that lies between Tory and the mainland,
or for the sky to be held up from the earth if it were falling on it, it would be done for them.'
(8) The Northern Saxons came to Ireland and plundered Mag Breg as far as Belach Dúin, and they took away with them a great body of captives, men and women.
The men of Ireland asked Adomnán to go to the Saxons to seek the return of their captives.
So Adomnán went to seek the captives. He put in at a great strand. Its ebb went out far and its flood came in fast.
This is how fast it was: when the flood tide begins, the best horse among the Saxons, under a good rider, with its back to the wave,
would only with difficulty carry its rider to land, swimming, because of how far the tide ebbed and how fast it flooded.
After that the Saxons would not let Adomnán come ashore on the strand.
'Put your boats on the strand,' said Adomnán to his community,
'for sea and land are subject to God's will, and nothing can be done apart from God.'
The clerics did as they had been told.
With his staff Adomnán drew a line around the boats, and God made the strand firm beneath the boats,
and made a high wall of the sea around them, so that they were on an island. The sea went past them as far as its limits and did them no harm.
When the Saxons saw that very great miracle, they began trembling for fear of Adomnán, and they granted him everything he wished.
Adomnán's wish was that all the captives be given to him, and that the Saxons never again go raiding in Ireland until Doomsday.
And Adomnán brought all the captives back.
(9) Once Adomnán was in the northern part of Mag Breg on a certain Sunday, that is,
in Uí Mac Uais. There he was given a hundred boiled sheep, and among them was a dog, which had also been boiled.
Through the grace of the Holy Spirit, Adomnán perceived the dog among the sheep.
And he said to the food-providers: 'Which of you gave us the dog among the sheep?'
Each of them swore separately that it was not he. Adomnán said to the dog:
"In the name of the Lord, get up quickly and show us your master."
At Adomnán's word the hound got up at once, leapt on its master and threw him to the ground.
Adomnán asked the man: "How many of you were involved in that deed?"
"Four of the Uí Chuirb," said the young man. And Adomnán said, cursing them:
"A curse in them and around them — it has put them away, it brings them from Uachtar Ard [?] — on the Uí Chuirb."
And he said that their kindred would never grow beyond four people until Judgement Day.
(10) Once the body of Bruide son of Bile, king of the Picts, was brought to Iona.
Adomnán felt grief and pain at his death. He said that Bruide's body should be brought to him in a house that night.
Adomnán kept watch over the body in that house until morning.
The next morning, when the body began to move and its eyes began to open,
a certain devout man came [?] to the door of the house and said:
"If Adomnán is expected to raise the dead, I say that no cleric who comes after him in his place shall be made abbot unless he raises the dead."
"There is something of justice in that," said Adomnán.
"Since it is more fitting, then, let us give a blessing to this body and to the soul of Bruide."
Bruide sent his spirit forth again to heaven with the blessing of Adomnán and of the community of Iona.
Then Adomnán said: "Many are the wonders that the King who was born of Mary works: life for Scuabán in Mull, death for Bruide son of Bile.
It is rare, after he has been king over a people, that a hollow stump of withered oak should enclose the son of the king of Dumbarton (Al Clud)."
(11) Another time Adomnán spent three days and three nights fasting in his closed house in Iona without coming into the monastery.
A few of the senior monks went to the house to see how the cleric was.
They looked through the keyhole and saw a very beautiful little boy in Adomnán's lap.
Adomnán was caressing the infant, so they were certain that it was Jesus who had come in the form of an infant to delight Adomnán.
(12) Another time, when Adomnán was in Iona, a body was brought to the island. A bell was rung there.
Everyone went out to meet it except Adomnán. When they reached the sea, the dead man rose up out of his hide-covered curragh and said to them:
"It would have been more fitting for you to look for a learned man to talk with me than to come out to meet me to bury me."
He put many wondrous questions to them. The questions were brought to Adomnán, and Adomnán answered them all.
"Ask Adamnán," he said,
"for he answers questions well, about a word that occurs in the baptism rite and what it means there, namely 'urget te Melthiel'."
They put this to Adamnán. Adamnán said: "That question was brought to Colum Cille from hell."
"And it is no wonder if Amelthiel is the name of the most deadly rank of demon."
"Open Colum Cille's oratory," said Adamnán.
This was done, and Adamnán made the sign of the cross toward the side where the body was.
The scream and wail of Satan were heard as he came out of the body on his way to hell.
(13) Preaching and teaching were among Adamnán's special gifts.
Then, in the last year of his life, he foretold to the men of Ireland and Scotland that a tribulation would come around this feast of John.
An unknown young warrior used to visit Colmán of Cruachan Aigle, that is,
an anchorite who lived in Connacht, and the young warrior used to tell Colmán many wonders,
and he said to him that Adamnán had foretold a tribulation for the men of Ireland and Scotland around this feast of John.
"Yes," said Colmán. "It will come true for him," said the young warrior,
"the tribulation is that Adamnán will go to heaven around this feast of John."
"It is great news and a great sorrow in the west of the world, and let that be sent from you to him," said the young warrior.
Colmán sent that message to Adamnán. "That is likely to be true," said Adamnán.
"Let us set out for our house in the name of God and of Colum Cille."
And afterwards he sang: If death should come to me in Iona, it would be a taking-hold of mercy.
I do not know, under blue heaven, a sod that would be better for a deathbed.
(14) A righteous man, then, was this man, with purity of nature like a patriarch. A true pilgrim like Abraham.
Gentle and forgiving from the heart like Moses. A praiseworthy psalmist like David.
A storehouse of wisdom like Solomon. A chosen vessel for proclaiming the truth like Paul the Apostle.
A man full of the grace and favour of the Holy Spirit like John the Youth.
A fair garden with plants of virtues. A fruitful branch of the vine.
A shining fire with glowing embers for warming and heating the sons of life by kindling charity and making it blossom.
A lion in strength and power. A dove in gentleness and simplicity.
A serpent in cunning and prudence toward good. Gentle, humble and kind toward the children of life.
Very grim and harsh toward the children of death. A slave of toil and service to Christ.
A king in dignity and power, for binding and loosing, for freeing and enslaving, for killing and bringing to life.
When the hour of death of the holy Adomnán drew near, he gave up his spirit to heaven, to the Lord whom he had served.
His body, however, remains here in the visible world for the present, with honour and veneration and with miracles every day.
Though his honour is great today, it will be greater on the Day of Judgement, when he will shine like the sun,
and judgement will be passed on the fruit of his teaching, of his good deeds, of his pilgrimage,
of his virginity and of his humility toward the Lord of the elements, in the union of the nine orders of heaven that did not transgress,
in the union of the saints and holy virgins of the world, of the patriarchs and prophets, and of the apostles and disciples of Jesus,
in the union of the divinity and humanity of the Son of God, in the union that is nobler than every other union,
in the union of the Holy Trinity, Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
I beseech the mercy of God through the intercession of Adomnán, that we may reach that union for ever and ever. Amen.
